verses.text: After these things, the butler of the king of Egypt and his baker offended their lord, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cup bearer and the chief baker.
He put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, into the prison, the place where Joseph was bound.
The captain of the guard assigned them to Joseph, and he took care of them. They stayed in prison many days.
They both dreamed a dream, each man his dream, in one night, each man according to the interpretation of his dream, the cup bearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were bound in the prison.
Joseph came in to them in the morning, and saw them, and saw that they were sad.
He asked Pharaoh’s officers who were with him in custody in his master’s house, saying, “Why do you look so sad today?”
They said to him, “We have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it.” Joseph said to them, “Don’t interpretations belong to God? Please tell it to me.”
The chief cup bearer told his dream to Joseph, and said to him, “In my dream, behold, a vine was in front of me,
and in the vine were three branches. It was as though it budded, it blossomed, and its clusters produced ripe grapes.
Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand; and I took the grapes, and pressed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.”
Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.
Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head, and restore you to your office. You will give Pharaoh’s cup into his hand, the way you did when you were his cup bearer.
But remember me when it will be well with you, and please show kindness to me, and make mention of me to Pharaoh, and bring me out of this house.
For indeed, I was stolen away out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the dungeon.”
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said to Joseph, “I also was in my dream, and behold, three baskets of white bread were on my head.
In the uppermost basket there were all kinds of baked food for Pharaoh, and the birds ate them out of the basket on my head.”
Joseph answered, “This is its interpretation. The three baskets are three days.
Within three more days, Pharaoh will lift up your head from off you, and will hang you on a tree; and the birds will eat your flesh from off you.”
On the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he made a feast for all his servants, and he lifted up the head of the chief cup bearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants.
He restored the chief cup bearer to his position again, and he gave the cup into Pharaoh’s hand;
but he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
Yet the chief cup bearer didn’t remember Joseph, but forgot him.

footnotes.content: The chapter opens with “after these things,” the same quiet hinge that has carried this story from one disaster to the next. Two of Pharaoh’s most trusted men, the one who held his cup and the one who set his bread before him, somehow offended their lord; the narrator never says how, and I have learned not to fill in what God left blank. High places sit close to the fire, and a king’s anger can end a man’s life in an afternoon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh’s anger falls on the cup bearer and the baker together, though their offenses may have been nothing alike. The text says only that he was angry, and two men who stood in his presence the day before are now waiting to learn whether they will live. Being near power is not the same as being safe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They are put into the custody of the captain of the guard, in the very prison where Joseph is bound — the same holding place attached to Potiphar’s house that we met two chapters back. The details are doing quiet work here: the cell God had already prepared for Joseph is now filling with the two men who stood nearest Pharaoh in the wine room and the kitchen. A prison was slowly becoming a waiting room for a palace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captain hands them over to Joseph, and the word is that he attended them — the same plain service he gave Potiphar’s household, now given to two disgraced officials. He did not know their case and they did not know his, and still he made their days bearable. Faithfulness had become a habit with him by then, which is the only way faithfulness ever becomes reliable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One night both men dream, each dream shaped to the man who dreamed it, and neither can read what he saw. God was speaking in an Egyptian prison to two men who did not know His name, and He spoke twice, as though to be sure the news would travel. He has always been able to hold a conversation with people who have not yet been introduced to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the morning Joseph comes in and reads their faces before he hears a single word. A man with his own unfinished grief — sold, slandered, and left to sit on a false charge — still had eyes for somebody else’s sadness. That is not natural to us; it is the sort of thing God grows slowly, in the dark, in a person who keeps looking outward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: “Why do you look so sad today?” he asks, and he calls them Pharaoh’s officers even though they are wearing prison clothes. He gives them back their dignity with a title, then opens a door with a question. Most people need to be asked before they will say what is heavy on them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: “Don’t interpretations belong to God?” Joseph answers, and that sentence keeps him honest for the rest of the chapter. Years later a prophet in Babylon will say the same thing in other words — there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries — and when Joseph finally stands before Pharaoh he will insist again, it is not in me. He had a gift, and he refused to carry it as though it were his own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cup bearer goes first, and the first thing he remembers is a vine standing in front of him. Not a throne, not a crowd — a vine, the one thing a man in that office would know with his own hands. God began with a picture from the man’s daily work, which is usually where He begins with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three branches bud, blossom, and ripen in one breath, a whole season folded into a moment. Dreams do that; they carry us faster than life does. But the God who set the growing seasons in order is not hurried by the three days this one pointed to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dream the man does exactly what he was trained to do: he takes the grapes, presses them into Pharaoh’s cup, and places the cup in Pharaoh’s hand. Before the dream came true he was given his calling back in miniature, the work itself folded into the promise. Sometimes the kindness of God is simply to let a person do their own good work again, even if only in a dream.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph answers without flinching: the three branches are three days. The counting is the easy part; the courage is in saying aloud what God has shown. He did not pad the answer or add a maybe, and he did not yet know whether the news would be good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: “Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office” — this is a phrase worth slowing down for. To lift up someone’s head in Scripture can mean to single them out, to count them, to show them favor; for this man it meant his old life handed back. In six verses Joseph will use those same words over the baker, and they will mean something terrible. One phrase, two men, and only God knew the difference.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now Joseph asks for something for himself, and it is the first personal request he has made in the whole story. Remember me, he says, show me kindness, mention me to Pharaoh, bring me out — four small imperatives from a man who had grabbed at nothing else, not Potiphar’s wife, not the keeper’s trust. He was not too proud to ask, and not confident enough to assume he would be heard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He tells his life in two sentences: I was stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here I have done nothing that deserves a dungeon. Notice what he leaves out — no accusation against Potiphar’s wife, no bitter retelling of the pit or the torn tunic, no naming of his brothers. He states his innocence and lets the record stay clean, which is a hard restraint for a man wronged twice over.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The baker hears that the interpretation was good and steps forward with his own dream, and you can almost hear the hope in him. Three baskets of white bread on my head, he says, as though the two dreams must belong to the same kind of day. It is very human to assume that mercy shown to the man beside you is a promise made to you.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He describes the top basket carefully: every kind of baked food for Pharaoh, the best of his craft, and birds eating out of it above his head. The detail is exact — bread was carried on the head in that country — and the dread is exact too. The one thing he could not guard was the thing just above his own eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph uses the same opening as before — this is its interpretation — and the three baskets are three days. He does not soften it, and he does not stall until the room empties. A man who has learned that the words are God’s will not edit them just because the editing would cost him something.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Within three days, Joseph says, Pharaoh will lift up your head from off you, and the birds will eat your flesh. It is the same phrase as verse thirteen, turned in the hand like a blade, and it must have taken real courage to speak it. Moses would later write that a man hanged on a tree is under a curse; I do not know whether Joseph was thinking of that, but I know the baker was not handed a gentler answer to make the room easier.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the third day Pharaoh keeps his birthday with a feast for all his servants, and he lifts up the head of both prisoners in front of the whole court. A royal birthday is a rare thing in Scripture; the next one I can recall ends with a prophet’s head on a platter. Here the gesture is identical for both men and the outcome splits them forever — one to a table, one to a tree.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cup bearer is restored, and the last detail is that the cup goes back into his hand. Everything Joseph said came true down to the cup, which should have made this man a witness and an advocate by evening. He went to bed holding the reminder of the prisoner who had given him his life back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The baker is hanged, and the narrator will not let us miss it: as Joseph had interpreted to them. The word spoken in the prison came to pass exactly, in the same three days, in the same court. It is a sober kind of proof — the interpreter is vindicated and a man is dead, and both things are true at once.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet the chief cup bearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him. Readers today hear an echo of every promise made in a hard season and quietly dropped — the call that never came back, the name never mentioned at the table, the door that stayed shut for two more years. As of 2026-10, I am grateful that we are not finally at the mercy of other people’s memory; there is One who says He will not forget, and He has never once lost a name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
